Learning Objectives
Review the anatomy and physiology of the Achilles tendon.
Explain the appropriate evaluation, diagnosis, and management of acute Achilles tendon
rupture.
Discuss the risks and advantages of surgical and nonsurgical management of acute Achilles
tendon rupture.
Describe the challenges associated with the management of chronic Achilles tendon ruptures.
Review various surgical techniques for the management of chronic Achilles tendon ruptures.
Introduction
The Achilles tendon is the largest tendon in the body and can withstand forces 12 times body
weight.

It is commonly ruptured during athletic activities and is not as frequently ruptured during
activities of daily living.
Ruptures occur in men and women throughout a broad age range, but most commonly occur
in individuals in their twenties to fifties.
The male-to-female ratio is 5:1.

Introduction
The Achilles tendon is the largest tendon in the body.1 It can withstand forces up to 12
times a person’s body weight and is essential for walking or running.1 Despite its size,
the Achilles tendon can rupture during activity,2 and rupture often occurs in young to
middle-aged men during sports and athletic endeavors.3 The injury is five times more
likely to occur in men than women.4 Although poorly understood, the incidence of
Achilles tendon injury is increasing.3,5 Treatment goals for acute Achilles tendon rupture
include restoring muscle integrity and tendon length, returning to full activity at
preinjury strength levels, and avoiding complications. Each patient’s goals, social factors,
and comorbidities must be considered in determining an individualized treatment plan.
Advances in nonsurgical treatment have created controversy regarding the management
of acute Achilles tendon ruptures, and a treatment consensus has not been achieved.
Anatomy
The Achilles tendon has the largest cross-sectional area of any tendon in the body.
It is formed from the gastrocnemius and soleus muscle as it converges and inserts onto the
calcaneal tuberosity.
The tendon twists 90° counterclockwise on the right side and clockwise on the left side as it
inserts into the calcaneus.
The primary blood supply is from the posterior tibial artery.
A hypovascular region of the tendon exists 2 to 6 cm from the insertion site. This is the most
common area of rupture.


Anatomy
The gastrocnemius muscle arises from the posterior aspect of the femur, with the lateral
head originating from the lateral femoral condyle and the medial head originating just
superior to the femoral condyle. The soleus arises from the soleal line and middle third
of the posterior tibia and the upper aspect of the posterior fibula, including the neck.
They converge to form the Achilles tendon and insert on the lateral and central calcaneal
tuberosity. On the right lower extremity, the last 6 cm of the tendon twists 90°
counterclockwise as it inserts on the calcaneus, and on the left lower extremity, the last
6 cm of the tendon twists 90° clockwise as it inserts on the calcaneus.6,7 The tendon is
perfused by the posterior tibial artery. Vascular supply to the distal tendon arises from
interosseous arterioles and proximally from the intramuscular arterial branches. A
hypovascular zone has been described 2 to 6 cm proximal to the calcaneal insertion, and
almost 75% of ruptures occur in this location7,8 (Figure 1).

Etiology
The mechanism of injury for Achilles tendon ruptures is indirect, and injury is caused by
tendon degeneration that leads to failure under mechanical load.
Three mechanisms of injury have been described:
Sharp unexpected dorsiflexion moment with a strong contraction of the gastrocnemius-
soleus complex
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:07 AM
AAOS | Achilles Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003000
4/37

Push-off weight bearing with knee extension
Substantial dorsiflexion moment on a plantarflexed ankle

Etiology
With continuous and rapid loading, the Achilles tendon behaves similar to a viscoelastic
material. As the modulus of elasticity increases, it becomes more stiff and, therefore,
prone to rupture.9 With tendon degeneration and these mechanical properties, the
tendon will fail under load. Most patients describe a noncontact injury. The proposed
mechanism of injury involves substantial loading of an already contracted
musculotendinous unit.10
Acute Rupture
Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients will report feeling a pop or a feeling of being struck from behind by an object or
opponent. In some patients, an audible pop can be heard.
Immediate weakness, swelling, and pain are noted; however, pain subsides relatively quickly.
A palpable gap may be noted by the examiner.
Patients will have a positive Thompson test. The examiner will squeeze the calf, and no plantar
flexion will occur with this maneuver.
If the patient is examined in the prone position with the knees flexed, the injured side will have
a more dorsiflexed resting position compared with the uninjured limb.

Patient History and Physical Examination
Many patients report feeling or hearing a pop in the Achilles tendon. Some patients
describe a feeling of being struck from behind by an opponent or object. Regardless,
these injuries are primarily noncontact injuries and may be missed. Patients will describe
immediate weakness, swelling, and pain; however, within several days, the pain
subsides. If examined in a timely fashion, patients will have a palpable gap at the level of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:07 AM
AAOS | Achilles Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003000
5/37

rupture, and an indentation may be visible if swelling has yet to occur or has subsided.
Plantar flexion weakness is easily elucidated; however, patients will have some plantar
flexion through the deep and lateral compartment muscles. If the patient is examined in
the prone position with the knees flexed, the injured side will have a resting carrying
angle in more dorsiflexion than that of the contralateral limb (Figure 2). Another method
for assessing this is by noting excessive dorsiflexion on the injured limb if patients can
tolerate such passive motion. Patients also will have a positive Thompson test.
Thompson and Doherty11 described this classic maneuver, in which squeezing the calf
will result in plantar flexion of the foot if the musculotendinous unit is intact. They noted
that in patients with an Achilles tendon rupture, the foot does not plantarflex with calf
squeeze, resulting in a positive test.11
Figure 2 Clinical photograph of lower legs of a patient with a left Achilles tendon rupture.
Note the increased dorsiflexion resting carrying angle of the left limb compared with the

contralateral limb. (Courtesy of Jeremy J. McCormick, MD, Chesterfield, MO.)
Imaging Studies
Imaging studies are not required in patients with positive physical examination findings.
MRI or ultrasonography can be performed if the diagnosis is uncertain or concomitant injuries
are suspected.

Imaging Studies
Positive physical examination findings and patient history rarely necessitate the need for
advanced imaging studies in patients with an Achilles tendon ruptures.8,12 The authors
of this lesson recommend obtaining a lateral ankle radiograph to assess for concomitant
tarsal bone fractures or an Achilles tendon sleeve avulsion (often noted as a proximally
migrated enthesophyte or calcification) because these injuries will affect management
(Figure 3). If concomitant soft-tissue injuries are suspected and the practitioner is unable
to confirm a diagnosis via physical examination, then ultrasonography or MRI can be
performed. Ultrasonography has been used to aid in identifying patients with a shorter
rupture gap, who are hypothesized to respond better to nonsurgical treatment;
however, this is controversial.13,14 Ultrasonography is a cheaper and readily available
imaging modality but is operator dependent. MRI is the preferred imaging modality for
Achilles tendon imaging, but it is expensive and often inconvenient for patients.

Achilles tendon sleeve avulsion. (Courtesy of Jeremy J. McCormick, MD, Chesterfield, MO.)
Nonsurgical Management
Modern nonsurgical management consists of functional bracing, early weight bearing, and
extensive physical therapy.
Functional outcomes of open repair and nonsurgical management have been shown to be
similar as early as 1 year after management.
Although re-rupture rates were thought to be higher with nonsurgical management, recent
studies have shown similar re-rupture rates between nonsurgical management and open
surgical repair.

Nonsurgical Management
Traditional nonsurgical management involved prolonged non–weight-bearing cast
immobilization, which was found to be inferior to surgical repair with regard to re-
rupture rates.2,15-18 A study of this treatment strategy demonstrated a higher rate of re-
rupture compared with surgical management (12.6% versus 3.5%, respectively).19
However, another level I study examining the differences between weight-bearing and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:07 AM
AAOS | Achilles Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003000
8/37

non–weight-bearing cast immobilization reported substantially lower re-rupture rates of
3% to 5%.20 The authors of that study excluded patients who sought treatment more
than 72 hours postinjury because hematoma could block tendon apposition. Some
surgeons argue that the exclusion of such patients may be the cause of the lower re-
rupture rates in that study. However, a retrospective review of 945 patients found that
re-rupture rates were similar between patients who underwent nonsurgical treatment
with an acute presentation and those who underwent treatment more than 2 weeks
postinjury (2.9% versus 2.7%, respectively; P = 0.13).21
Proponents of modern early functional rehabilitation argue that such treatment is
associated with significantly lower re-rupture rates compared with cast
immobilization2,17,22 and is comparable to surgical management.17,18,22-25 With this
treatment modality, a plantarflexed brace or controlled ankle motion walking boot are
used for immobilization, and range of motion and weight bearing are initiated earlier
than with traditional, non–weight-bearing nonsurgical management.26 A recent meta-
analysis of 10 randomized controlled trials consisting of 418 patients treated surgically
and 408 patients treated nonsurgically via early functional rehabilitation found no
statistically significant difference in the risk of rupture between the cohorts (absolute risk
difference, 1.7%; P = 0.45).17 In a randomized controlled study of 97 patients who
underwent surgical treatment or early functional rehabilitation, no difference in
functional testing or Achilles tendon Total Rupture Score27 (a validated patient-reported
outcome measure) was noted 1 year postoperatively.22 In this same study, functional
testing was superior in the surgical group at a follow-up of 6 months; however, fewer
differences were noted at a follow-up of 1 year. Neither group had the treated limb
reach the functional capacity of the uninjured limb.22 In a level II prospective
comparative study of 200 patients, no difference in Achilles tendon Total Rupture Scores
at a follow-up of 2 years was noted between surgical and nonsurgical management via
an identical functional rehabilitation protocol. In addition, a regression analysis found no
effect of patient age (18 to 65 years), sex, or mode of treatment on Achilles tendon Total
Rupture Scores.
Regardless, successful nonsurgical management requires compliance and access to a
physical therapist familiar with and capable of implementing a bracing and functional
rehabilitation protocol. To date, researchers continue to debate whether modern
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:07 AM

9/37

nonsurgical management results in truly similar re-rupture rates and return to activity
compared with surgical management.
Surgical Management
Open Repair
Open surgical repair involves a larger incision through which the ruptured Achilles tendon
ends are débrided, if necessary, and reapproximated with the use of suture material.
Historically, re-rupture rates were thought to be substantially lower with surgical repair than
with nonsurgical management, and functional outcomes were favorable.
The risk for wound healing complications, which occur in 5% to 10% of patients, is high.

Open Repair
Proponents of open repair argue that it results in better strength, endurance, and more
equal restoration of calf circumference compared with nonsurgical
management.15,18,22,25 In a level IV ultrasonographic study, 50% of Achilles tendon tear
defects could not be compensated for via plantar flexion immobilization alone.28 Tendon
length is known to be inversely proportional to muscle strength,29 and restoration of
length via surgical management may aid in achieving a more satisfactory outcome.
In a level II meta-analysis, surgical repair was shown to be superior to nonsurgical
management in terms of jumping and endurance testing (P < 0.05).25 In this study, no
difference was found between the groups with regard to ability to return to previous
level of sports activity.25 A level I randomized controlled trial of 60 patients found that
surgical management resulted in faster and better recovery of calf muscle strength
throughout the entire muscle arc at a follow-up of 6 and 18 months.15 The postoperative
rehabilitation protocol was identical between groups. Four re-ruptures were noted in the
nonsurgical group versus one re-rupture in the surgical group. Only one infection was
noted in the surgical group.15 In a level II study that analyzed the effect of early weight
bearing in a nonsurgical management cohort, the injured limb was found to perform
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:07 AM
AAOS | Achilles Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003000
10/37

40% less work than the uninjured limb.30 In this same study, improvement ceased at 6
months postinjury. A level I study on management showed that muscle strength,
endurance, and patient-reported outcomes continued to improve as long as 12 months
postoperatively but did not normalize compared with the contralateral limb.31
Comparing these two studies suggests that patients treated surgically have the capacity
to improve over a longer period than patients treated nonsurgically. In addition, a level I
study showed that return to work was faster in surgically treated patients; however,
minimal difference was found in re-rupture rates and functional outcomes in comparing
surgical management with nonsurgical management consisting of functional
rehabiliation.17
Multiple studies have reported lower re-rupture rates in surgical groups.2,15-18 A recent
level II meta-analysis showed that re-rupture rates are lower with surgical management;
however, differences are small (risk difference, 1.6%).24 Many of these studies include
patients who were treated via open repair. Open repair is advantageous because it is
biomechanically stronger than minimally invasive repair3 and allows for the use of an
epitenon stitch, which reduces repair site gapping and increases strength.32-37
Therefore, a stronger construct may theoretically result in a more predictable and faster
rehabilitation.
Surgical repair often is successful, but it is associated with a high rate of complications,
including infection and impaired wound healing.19,24 A recent level I meta-analysis
comparing surgical repair with nonsurgical management reported a substantial risk
difference of 3.3%.24 In this study, re-rupture rates were equal between the cohorts.24 In
addition, surgical management is more expensive than nonsurgical management. In a
level I cost-effectiveness analysis study, surgical management was weakly cost-effective
(57% likelihood), with a cost of 50,000 Euros per quality-adjusted life year.38
Percutaneous Repair
Percutaneous Achilles tendon repair techniques involve the use of instrumentation to pass
and secure sutures through ruptured tendon ends, with substantially smaller incisions and
less tissue disruption.

Compared with open repair, percutaneous Achilles tendon repair techniques have resulted in
fewer complications with similar patient outcomes.
Wound cosmesis and irritation is improved with percutaneous Achilles tendon repair.
Compared with open repair, higher risks of sural nerve injury have been reported with
percutaneous repair.

Percutaneous Repair
Minimally invasive or percutaneous repair techniques may result in decreased re-
rupture rates with substantially fewer complications39-41 compared with open repair
(Figure 4). Therefore, these treatment modalities are gaining favor. A recent
retrospective comparative study (level III) found that open and minimally invasive repair
techniques resulted in similar functional outcomes, isokinetic variables, and calf
circumference.42 In a meta-analysis of eight studies that included 358 patients treated
via minimally invasive repair or open repair, Grassi et al40 reported a decreased risk ratio
of 0.21 (95% confidence interval = 0.10 to 0.40; P = 0.00001) for overall complications and
0.15 (95% confidence interval = 0.05 to 0.46; P = 0.0009) for wound infection, favoring
minimally invasive repair. The authors also found that patients treated via minimally
invasive repair were more likely to have good or excellent subjective results in terms of
patient-reported outcomes (risk ratio = 1.18; 95% confidence interval = 1.04 to 1.33; P =
0.009).40

In a level III study of 270 patients, patients treated via percutaneous repair had a higher
rate of return to preinjury level of activity at 5 months postoperatively.43 The 101
patients who underwent percutaneous repair had similar functional results and no
substantial differences in complications at a mean follow-up of 9 months compared with

either group, and no instances of deep infection or sural neuritis were noted in the

(2%), and sural neuritis occurred in five patients (3%).43 In a meta-analysis of 13 studies
that included 854 patients who underwent open or minimally invasive Achilles tendon
repair, Alcelik et al39 found no difference in return to sports activity between the two
cohorts. In this study, re-rupture rates and rates of sural nerve injury were not
statistically different. Substantially more complications were found in the open repair

group compared with the minimally invasive group (109 versus 32, respectively; P =
0.00001).39
Chronic Rupture
Chronic Achilles tendon ruptures can result from missed diagnosis, unrecognized injury, or
delayed presentation.
The goal of management is to restore appropriate length and tension to the
musculotendinous unit of the Achilles tendon.
Surgical management is the main treatment option, with surgical technique generally selected
based on the length of the Achilles tendon defect.

Chronic Rupture
A patient with a chronic Achilles tendon rupture poses a unique challenge in treatment.
Chronic ruptures commonly result from a missed diagnosis, unrecognized injury, or
delayed presentation. As many as 25% of acute Achilles tendon ruptures are not
diagnosed at the initial clinical visit.44 The already difficult management of Achilles
tendon rupture is made more complex by the delayed presentation because of the
variability in tendon condition.
Management of chronic Achilles tendon rupture is dictated by patient comorbidities and
functional goals, with nonsurgical treatment typically reserved for low-demand patients
or patients who cannot safely tolerate surgical treatment. Factors such as age, activity
level, defect size, body habitus, soft-tissue envelope, and medical comorbidities should
be considered in selection of the treatment strategy.45 Surgical management is the main
treatment option, and several surgical techniques have been described. The goal of
surgical management is to maximize function by restoring the appropriate length and
tension to the musculotendinous unit of the Achilles tendon. Surgical decision making
typically has been driven by the length of the tendon defect as estimated on MRI and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:07 AM
AAOS | Achilles Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003000
14/37

visualized intraoperatively. Several algorithms based on expert opinion have been
published in the literature.46-49
Patient History and Physical Examination
A patient with a chronic Achilles tendon rupture may not have much pain or a recent
description of injury.
A patient with a chronic Achilles tendon rupture will have weakness with plantar flexion,
inability to perform a single-limb heel rise, and fatigue with repetitive motion.
Because of scar tissue formation, patients with a chronic Achilles tendon rupture may not have
a palpable gap.
A Thompson test may show a plantar flexion response because of scar tissue formation at the
site of rupture; however, it will be less vigorous than the response on the uninjured side.
Loss of normal resting tension in the prone position is a key finding in patients with a chronic
Achilles tendon rupture.

Patient History and Physical Examination
The presentation of a patient with a chronic Achilles tendon rupture is different than that
of a patient with an acute rupture. A patient with an acute injury may describe a recent
injury with a feeling of a pop at the posterior aspect of the ankle, whereas a patient with
a chronic rupture may not remember an episode of injury. The initial pain and swelling
of the acute rupture often have subsided in patients with a chronic presentation. Often,
the patient will have seen a provider for evaluation and not have received a diagnosis of
Achilles tendon rupture.44 Patients with a chronic injury primarily report weakness with
loss of push-off strength, difficulty ascending and descending stairs, or inability to
elevate to the toes on the injured side. The patient often will notice a limp when
walking.49
The physical examination should consist of a typical neurovascular examination with
palpation of pulses and evaluation of sensation through the foot and ankle. All motor
groups should be examined for appropriate function and strength. Plantar flexion

strength typically will be diminished; however, the other muscles of the posterior
compartment of the leg will maintain some ability to plantarflex. The patient likely will
not be able to perform a single-limb heel rise and will fatigue with repetitive motion.46 In
addition, because the tendon has had time to heal, a palpable gap in the tendon may not
be present because scar tissue may be filling that gap (Figure 5).
Figure 5 Clinical photograph of an ankle shows the posterior skin and soft-tissue
contracture characteristic of a chronic Achilles tendon rupture. (Reproduced from
Schweitzer KM Jr, Dekker TJ, Adams SB: Chronic Achilles ruptures: Reconstructive
options. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2018;26[21]:753-763.)
Physical examination in the prone position is critically important in the patient
evaluation. The classic Thompson test demonstrates loss of plantar flexion of the foot
with squeeze of the calf because of disruption of the Achilles tendon.50 A patient with a
chronic rupture may show some plantar flexion response with squeeze of the calf
because scar tissue may have formed between the ruptured tendon ends, restoring
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:07 AM
AAOS | Achilles Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003000
16/37

some continuity to the tendon. Typically, any plantar flexion movement on the injured
side will be less vigorous than that on the uninjured side. Comparison of resting
positions of the feet in the prone position via the Matles test will help visualize the loss of
tension through the Achilles tendon on the injured side, resulting in a more dorsiflexed
resting position of the foot.51
Imaging Studies
MRI aids in estimating the size of the defect and the quality of the gastrocnemius-soleus
muscle belly in patients with a chronic Achilles tendon rupture.

Imaging Studies
Radiographs can be obtained in the initial evaluation of chronic Achilles tendon ruptures
to rule out an Achilles tendon avulsion. Ultrasonography also may be helpful because it
is an inexpensive and quick imaging modality to evaluate the tendon. Ultrasonography is
operator dependent and, therefore, may afford variable assistance in evaluating a
chronic Achilles tendon rupture.52 MRI typically is the most helpful imaging modality. It
can help estimate the magnitude of the defect between the normal tendon ends, which
will help guide management, particularly selection of the surgical reconstruction
technique. In addition, the muscle belly can be evaluated to identify fatty infiltration or
fibrosis that may lead to difficulty regaining complete function. In such situations,
tendon transfer may be helpful.
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management of chronic Achilles tendon ruptures typically is reserved for low-
demand patients or patients with substantial medical comorbidities.

Nonsurgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:07 AM
AAOS | Achilles Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003000
17/37

Patients with a chronic Achilles tendon rupture have approximately 36% of normal
plantar flexion compared with the uninjured side, which is difficult to restore via
nonsurgical management.53 Therefore, nonsurgical treatment of a chronic Achilles
tendon rupture typically is reserved for low-demand patients; patients with substantial
medical comorbidities, such as poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, smoking, or
peripheral vascular disease; and patients in whom noncompliance is a concern.54
Historically, nonsurgical management of acute Achilles tendon ruptures consisted of
serial cast immobilization with progressive ankle dorsiflexion. Recent studies have
supported a more aggressive functional rehabilitation protocol with good results.55
However, these studies have examined acute Achilles tendon ruptures. To the
knowledge of the authors of this lesson, no studies have examined nonsurgical
management of chronic Achilles tendon ruptures via a functional rehabilitation protocol.
Surgical Management
Surgical management is guided by the length of the Achilles tendon defect as measured
preoperatively on MRI or identified intraoperatively.

Surgical Management
No preferred or scientifically defined strategy exists for the management of chronic
Achilles tendon ruptures. Outcome studies are largely case series. Expert opinion has led
to published surgical treatment algorithms largely based on the size of the defect.46-49
One such algorithm is the Myerson classification46 (Table 1). Type 1 defects are 1 to 2 cm
long and can be managed via direct end-to-end repair. Type 2 defects are 2 to 5 cm long
and are managed via tendon-lengthening procedures, such as V-Y lengthening of the
gastrocnemius-soleus complex, and possibly a tendon transfer. Type 3 defects are
longer than 5 cm and are managed via tendon transfer with or without local tendon
lengthening (V-Y or turndown technique).

230.
Direct Repair
Direct end-to-end repair can be used to manage chronic Achilles tendon ruptures with a gap of
less than 2 cm between the tendon ends.
If a chronic rupture can be adequately débrided to restore appropriate tension to the tendon
and then can be repaired, incorporating scar tissue into the tendon repair, a good result can
be achieved.

Direct Repair
Direct end-to-end repair of chronic Achilles tendon ruptures often is difficult. At the time
of presentation, the tendon defect has healed with fibrous scar tissue. If the tendon
defect is smaller than 2 cm after débridement of the interposed tissue, then end-to-end
repair without tendon transfer is feasible. Scar tissue surrounding the proximal stump
must be released, and traction should be applied to gently stretch the tissues so that
end-to-end apposition can be achieved. Each end of the tendon can be captured with the
use of a heavy, nonabsorbable suture that is fastened at the tendon end. This repair site
is then oversewn with the use of an absorbable suture to reinforce the repair. The
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:07 AM
AAOS | Achilles Tendon Disorders
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003000
19/37

paratenon should be repaired as a separate layer, if possible, to enhance healing and
avoid excessive scar formation. If excessive plantar flexion (>30°) is necessary to oppose
the tendon ends, the repair may not heal adequately because of substantial tension. In
this situation, proximal V-Y lengthening should be performed.54
Porter et al56 described a technique for end-to-end repair in which débridement of
interposed scar tissue was limited and some of the remaining tissue was incorporated
into the tendon repair. At a mean of 47 days postinjury, 11 patients underwent end-to-
end repair via this technique. Excellent functional outcomes and no re-ruptures were
reported at a mean follow-up of 18 months. Yasuda et al57 published results on a similar
technique, preserving interposed scar tissue and incorporating it into end-to-end repair
of a chronically ruptured tendon. In their study, 30 patients had no re-ruptures and no
difficulty with walking and ascending stairs at a mean follow-up of 33 months.
V-Y Tendon Advancement
Chronic Achilles tendon ruptures with a gap of 2 to 5 cm between the tendon ends can be
reconstructed via V-Y tendon advancement.
This technique results in plantar flexion weakness and often is augmented with flexor hallucis
longus (FHL) tendon transfer to strengthen the reconstruction.
Despite some persistent weakness, patients typically are satisfied with their outcomes.

V-Y Tendon Advancement
If the tendon defect is 2 to 5 cm in length after débridement, V-Y lengthening of the
gastrocnemius-soleus fascia may be required.46 With this technique, an inverted V-
shaped incision is made in the Achilles tendon fascia near the musculotendinous
junction. The incision is made only through the tendinous portion of the gastrocnemius-
soleus complex. Each limb of the V-shaped incision should be 1.5 to 2 times the length of
the defect in the tendon.58 The apex of the V-shaped incision should be at the proximal
aspect of the musculotendinous junction. After the proximal stump of the tendon
rupture is débrided, a heavy, nonabsorbable suture is placed in this stump. Traction is

Although this technique restores continuity to the tendon, it disrupts the
musculotendinous unit and often results in weakness with plantar flexion.56,58-60 As
much as a 30% deficit in plantar flexion strength compared with the uninjured side has
been reported.59 Because of this weakness, V-Y tendon advancement typically is
augmented with a tendon transfer. The most common tendon transferred is the FHL.
After tendon transfer, the resulting reconstruction and repair typically is still weak, with a
peak torque deficit of as much as 22.3%.58 Despite this weakness, patients report good
outcome scores, suggesting a high rate of satisfaction with the procedure.58,61

Turndown Flap
If the chronic Achilles tendon rupture has a resultant defect of more than 5 cm, then a
gastrocnemius-soleus fascia turndown flap is most helpful to reconstruct the defect.
Several techniques have been used with good clinical success; however, reconstruction with a
turndown flap typically results in loss of plantar flexion strength and, therefore, is commonly
augmented via tendon transfer.

Turndown Flap
If a chronic Achilles tendon rupture has a defect of more than 5 cm between the tendon
ends after débridement of interposed scar tissue, then a gastrocnemius-soleus
turndown flap can be used for reconstruction of the Achilles tendon. A midline approach
is extended proximally to expose the gastrocnemius-soleus fascia. The gap in the
Achilles tendon is measured after débridement with the knee at 90° and the foot in
simulated resting plantar flexion. The distally based flap is then fashioned, with a cuff of
1 to 2 cm left attached at the distal end of the fascia (Figure 7). The flap typically is 1 to 3
cm in width and as long as 12 cm.60,62,63 The proximal flap is then turned downward,
deep into tissue, and is passed distally to join with the distal stump. The pedicle of the
flap is reinforced with the use of suture to avoid complete avulsion.54 At this point, a
heavy, nonabsorbable suture is used to capture the proximal turndown flap and repair it
to a similar suture through the distal stump of the chronic rupture. If the flap has excess
length, then the tendons can overlap. The proximal defect left by the flap harvest is
sutured together with the use of an absorbable suture. The paratenon is then closed in a
separate layer, if possible, and the skin is closed carefully.

chronic Achilles tendon defect have been described with good success.66,67 Similar to V-
Y tendon advancement, turndown reconstruction typically leads to decreased plantar
flexion strength and, therefore, is augmented via tendon transfer, most commonly the

Tendon Transfers
Tendon transfers are an important adjunct to chronic Achilles tendon reconstruction,
particularly to address the loss of plantar flexion strength associated with V-Y lengthening and
turndown graft procedures.
The FHL is the most common tendon transferred in the reconstruction of chronic Achilles
tendon injuries because of its phase of action (in phase with the Achilles tendon), line of pull,
and biomechanical strength.
The FHL harvest technique may involve one incision through the posterior ankle or two
incisions, including a medial approach to the foot and transection at the knot of Henry.
Numerous fixation methods can be used for tendon transfer. Most commonly, fixation
involves incorporation into the chronic Achilles tendon repair, a bone tunnel, and interference
screw fixation.

Tendon Transfers
Although end-to-end repair, V-Y lengthening, and turndown grafts can bridge the gap of
a chronic Achilles tendon rupture, the loss of strength associated with these procedures
suggests that tendon transfer also should be performed. The ideal tendon transfer
offers local collagen to reinforce the repair construct, increases vascularity to the repair
construct, and adds dynamic strength.68 Ideally, the tendon should function in the same
phase of the gait cycle as the Achilles tendon to minimize retraining of the tendon during
rehabilitation. The FHL, the flexor digitorum longus, and the peroneus brevis are options
for tendon transfer in patients undergoing chronic Achilles tendon reconstruction.69-73
The FHL is the most common tendon transferred during Achilles tendon reconstruction
because of its phase of action, line of pull, and biomechanical strength.74
Hansen69 first described the use of the FHL tendon for Achilles tendon reconstruction.
The technique was then popularized by Wapner et al,70 who performed a long tendon
harvest by making a medial incision on the foot, transecting the FHL at the knot of
Henry. The tendon is pulled out through the posterior Achilles tendon incision and
transferred through the calcaneus, anterior to the insertion of the Achilles tendon
stump. With the advent of biotenodesis screws, which allow for reliable fixation through
a bone tunnel in the calcaneus, a short harvest of the FHL tendon, with the tendon

Other Graft Options
Allograft can be successfully used to reconstruct chronic Achilles tendon ruptures in patients
with a massive defect.
Autograft tendons have been considered in the reconstruction of chronic Achilles tendon
ruptures; however, use of autograft reconstruction has decreased because of donor site
morbidity and the reliability of tendon transfers.
The use of synthetic grafts in chronic Achilles tendon reconstruction has been studied;
however, they should be used with caution.


shown to improve function and result in return to activity. In a study of 14 patients who

Another allograft that has been studied is acellular dermal human matrix in the form of
a patch. This skin allograft has been used as a wrap surrounding end-to-end repair,

Autograft tendons also can be used for chronic Achilles tendon reconstruction. Viable
options include the semitendinosus, gracilis, quadriceps, and fascia lata;83-86 however,
none of these grafts has been shown to be the preferred method for repair because the
literature supporting these techniques consists of case series, with various autograft
reconstruction approaches being described.

reconstructions, such as knotted monofilament polypropylene mesh, polyester tape,

have been evaluated in case series, with no single option showing substantial benefit

Conclusion
The Achilles tendon is the largest and most commonly ruptured tendon in the human body.
This injury most commonly occurs in men aged 30 to 40 years.
Diagnosis often is made based on a through patient history and physical examination, with
little need for advanced imaging studies.
Nonsurgical management of acute Achilles tendon ruptures is effective and appropriate in
select patients if early functional rehabilitation can be provided and the patient can be
followed with adequate regularity and physical therapy support.
Evidence suggests that surgical repair is acceptable in healthy and active patients who want to
recover as fast as possible and is associated with a reduced risk of re-rupture. In addition,
surgical repair may be preferred if a high level of physical activity is desired.
Less invasive repair techniques may be more advantageous than open repair because they
result in similar outcomes with decreased complication rates.
Chronic Achilles tendon ruptures may result from a missed diagnosis, unrecognized injury, or
delayed presentation.
Surgical management is the main treatment option for chronic Achilles tendon ruptures, with
the goal of restoring appropriate length and tension to the tendon.
Nonsurgical management of chronic Achilles tendon ruptures is reserved for patients with low
demands or substantial medical comorbidities.
The size of the defect in a patient with a chronic Achilles tendon rupture will help guide
surgical decision making.
A defect of smaller than 2 cm can be managed via direct end-to end repair. A defect of 2 to 5
cm can be managed via V-Y tendon advancement with tendon transfer augmentation. A defect
larger than 5 cm can be managed via a turndown flap reinforced with a tendon transfer.
The FHL is the most common tendon transferred. Allograft, autograft, and synthetic grafts also
have been described.
